Abstract
Here we report the development of SPRAY, a masively paralel GPU acelerated,
smothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH)-based, radiation hydrodynamics (RHD) code
designed specicaly for simulating high intensity laser-plasma interactions. When a
target is iradiated by an intense laser, highly complex uid deformation ocurs due
to instabilities, which is chalenging to study numericaly. SPRAY is particle-based,
mesh-fre, and Lagrangian, which adreses numerical isues that posed diculties
to existing methods. Its SPH formulations for RHD governing equations are tailored
toward acurate and reliable simulations of laser-target iradiation phenomena, and
are solved via a time-dependent, ux-limited diusion method. A new laser energy
coupling module, which is based on the Wentzel-Kramers-Brilouin (WKB) aproxi-
mation, is implemented with a totaly mesh-fre ray-tracing scheme that is aplicable
for arbitrary geometry and dimensions. The acuracy and reliability of the code are
demonstrated with a series of benchmark problems. To the authors’ knowledge, this is
the rst atempt to employ SPH method for simulations of laser-plasma interactions in
high energy density physics research. Posible expansions to the code, such as laser
beam-beam interaction modeling and more sophisticated multi-group radiation trans-
port are left for future development.
1. Introduction
The interaction of high-intensity lasers with plasmas, both experimentaly and nu-
mericaly, is a popular research topic since the early days of high energy density physics
(HEDP) and inertial connement fusion (ICF) research. The simulation of high energy
density plasmas, characterized by high presure (typicaly greater than 1 Mbar), is key
to our understanding of stelar interiors and astrophysical systems [1, 2, 3]. Moreover,
ICF experiments, which aim to produce nuclear fusion reactions by garnering the po-
tentials of HEDPs, continue to show promising results on the path to realizing fusion
energy production [4].

In laboratory setings, high energy density plasmas, including laser-driven ICF
plasmas, are produced by iradiating solid targets with high-intensity lasers, typicaly

corona plasmas are formed as a result of ablation, and high compresion regions are
created by shock waves. In adition, a host of instabilities is induced due to step pres-
sure and density gradients. Ablative Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities (ARTI), for instance,
ocur in both the ablation front and the boundary betwen the fuel and the hot-spot,
and it is esential to control and mitigate such phenomena as they seriously degrade the
ICF performance [5, 6]. However, the multi-scale nature of these physical phenomena
poses chalenges to experimental diagnosis and analysis. Therefore, it is of great inter-
est to study the interactions betwen high-intensity lasers and plasmas with numerical
analysis.
There are a variety of numerical aproaches available to examine high-intensity
laser-plasma interactions. Eulerian-based methods [7, 8, 9], although wel-established
and numericaly matured, pose diculties in tracking the moving multi-uid interfaces
due to their grid-based nature. In adition, when the coronal plasma expands as ab-
lation progreses, it becomes chalenging to kep track of the boundary surface of the
plasma. Moreover, adaptive mesh renement (AMR) schemes, which are necesary
to resolve the ne spatial structures of instabilities, are computationaly intensive. On
the other hand, there exist a number of codes [10, 1, 12, 13] that take the Lagrangian
aproach to avoid these isues. In these aproaches, the plasma boundary is trivialy
tracked as the Lagrangian uid elements move in space. However, these codes are gen-
eraly cel-based, meaning that the uid elements are represented by stagered cels.
This severely limits the ability to handle large uid deformations that are comon-
place in hydrodynamic instabilities in the context of HEDPs.
In this paper, an aplication of particle-based, mesh-fre, Lagrangian aproach
to solve radiation hydrodynamics (RHD) is presented. SPRAY (Smothed Particle
RAdiation hYdrodynamics), a SPH-based RHD code, is developed specicaly for
high-intensity laser-plasma interaction simulations. It is, to our knowledge, the rst
SPH code to model such phenomena with detailed physical modeling and material data.
SPH, rst proposed independently by Lucy [14] and Gingold and Monaghan [15], is a
particle-based hydrodynamics method, as the name sugests. It does not rely on any
mesh, grid or cel to numericaly solve hydrodynamics governing equations, and it is
Lagrangian in nature, as the uid elements are tracked by particles. The strengths and
advantages of SPH come from its ability to handle multi-uid dynamics with complex
deformations. Because of its versatility and robustnes, it is being utilized not only by
scientic comunities but also in industrial aplications, as evidenced by the continued
publications of a series of review papers [16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 2, 23, 24, 25].
Since SPH was rst developed for and aplied to astrophysical problems, there
has ben a continued interest in incorporating radiation transport modeling into the
SPH formulation. In particular, modeling ionizing radiation has ben atempted by nu-
merous studies, mostly by ray-tracing ionizing photons emited by radiation sources
[26, 27, 28, 29]. There also have ben studies where the domain is discretized into vir-
tual cones in order to preserve the directed transport [30]. However, these aproaches
are highly expensive in terms of computation, and require generation and tracking of
virtual photon particles. Because of these shortcomings, there also has ben another
2


branch in radiation transport modeling in SPH using the ux-limited diusion aprox-
imation derived by [31]. The diusion aproximation takes the zeroth moment of the
radiation transport equation and is valid when the opacity is not to smal. Studies
that employ this aproximation include [32, 3, 34]. In adition, moment-based ap-
proaches with variable Edington tensor aproximation for opticaly thin regime have
ben proposed as wel [35]. Recently, there has ben a novel study that proposes solv-
ing both the zeroth and the rst moment simultaneously, dubed the two-moment
method [36].
Because SPRAY is a RHD code targeting laser-plasma interactions, the physical
characteristics of laser-driven plasmas were taken into consideration when designing
the radiation transport scheme. Because the optical depth of laser-produced plasma is
generaly thick, the use of ux-limited diusion aproximation is justied, so we opted
to take this aproach for the sake of computational eciency. In adition, because
the hydrodynamics of the laser-plasma interactions neded to be resolved at the same
time, RHD is solved via operator spliting method where radiation transport is solved
implicitly and hydrodynamics is solved explicitly [3, 37, 38, 39]. Furthermore, the
radiation transport equations are coupled to the thre-temperature description of plasma
(ion, electron, and radiation) instead of the one- or at most two-temperature description
used in previous studies, because of the large discrepancy betwen ion and electron
temperatures during high intensity laser-plasma interactions.
In SPRAY, laser energy deposition in plasma is described by the inverse bremstrahlung
absorption model [40], and it is numericaly implemented in the Wentzel-Kramers-
Brilouin (WKB) aproximation form [41]. The WKB aproximation is valid when
the laser wavelength is shorter than the plasma gradient scale length, and this condition
is satised for long pulse lasers with pulse duration in the order of nanoseconds, which
are the main target of this research [41]. The novelty of SPRAY’s laser ray-tracing
module lies in the fact that it is coupled to a particle-based mesh-fre SPH method, un-
like the de facto mesh-based ray-tracing routine developed by [42] and implemented in
state-of-the-art codes like FLASH [7] and HYDRA [13]. It also uses equation-of-state
(EOS) data generated by MPQEOS [43] and opacity data from SNOP [4]. The EOS
data is neded for the closure of hydrodynamic equations, and the opacity data, which
describes the emision and absorption of radiation, is required for radiation transport
calculations. SPRAY is coded in CUDA C/C+, which enables masively paralel
execution on NVIDIA GPUs, and is developed on the basis of a wel-established nu-
clear thermal-hydraulics code SOPHIA [45, 46]. Several key modules from SOPHIA,
such as the GPU-paralelized nearest neighbor particle search (NPS) algorithm, along
with the predictor-corector time integration scheme and output le generation routine,
were used as the building blocks for SPRAY. The details of numerical methods are pre-
sented in Section 2, code benchmark results are shown in Section 3, and conclusions
are drawn in Section 4.

2.4. Fre surface boundary
SPH was originaly developed to study astrophysical plasmas, where boundaries
are neglected. The lack of clear delineations of surfaces like in mesh-based aproaches
makes boundaries a non-trivial isue [24]. In the formulation of SPH equations, it is
asumed that sucient particles are present within the kernel suport domain (refer
to equation (4). However, on or near the boundary, the truncation of the SPH ker-
nel, i.e. particle deciency, leads to inacurate interpolation, thus compromising the
acuracy of the calculation. There have ben numerous studies proposing solutions
to this isue, including the Shepard lter [67], kernel gradient corection (KGC) [62],
corective smothed particle method (CSPM) [68], and nite particle method (FPM)
[69]. Although these methods are shown to be robust and versatile in many aplica-
tions, they are not suitable for frely expanding surfaces where the variation of density
is very dramatic and the gradient on the boundary surface could be very step.
When simulating laser iradiation of a target, the target surface undergoes ablation,
and a rapidly expanding coronal plasma is formed. As a result, a step gradient is
formed in the physical proles (density, presure, velocity, etc.) where the dierence
in density over a few dozen SPH particles apart can be in the order of 10

poses unique chalenges in boundary treatment, since the SPH aproximation would
result in underestimation of the gradient due to lack of sucient information. In other

boring particles are on the ater side of the gradient.
There have ben atempts to adres similar problems. Reinhardt et al. [70] sug-
gested using a corection factor that is determined a priori by numerical ting of the
sample data. The esence of this scheme is to estimate the true gradient based on the
corected volume of each particle, which is determined based on an imbalance factor
that holds the information of the particle distribution. The shortcomings of this ap-
proach not only include the isue where the numerical ting neds to be performed
every time a dierent kernel function is chosen, but also lie in the fact that this is es-
sentialy an a posteriori x with limited physical justications. Therefore, the utility of
this scheme is highly dependent on the characteristics of the problem at hand, and was
shown to be limited in acuracy in our testing. On the other hand, Ruiz-Bonila et al.

3.5. Laser driven inertial connement fusion target compresion simulation - Mesh-

One of the most popular topics in the high-intensity laser-plasma interaction re-
search is the laser-driven inertial connement fusion (ICF). By iradiating the ablator
material with high power lasers, the ablation pushes the DT fuel inward, causing the
target capsule to implode. Therefore, the coupling betwen the laser energy deposition
routine and the plasma simulation is critical to the sucesful numerical modeling of
this experiment. Here, a laser driven compresion of a ICF target is simulated with
SPRAY to verify its laser ray-tracing scheme and its integration to the code.
The simulation setup is similar to that of ref. [87]. A thin cylindrical shel of DT
ice with iner radius of 1.76 m and outer radius of 1.934 m is coated with a ablator
layer composed of polystyrene (CH) with a thicknes of 0.037 m. The interior of the
shel is asumed to be led with low density DT gas. A 250 nm wavelength laser is set
to uniformly iradiate the target at 50 TW of power, and 2048 rays are used in total.
Because the nuclear fusion reaction of DT is not modeled in this code, the simulation
is set to terminate before the deceleration phase begins. The option to solve radiation
transport was disabled in this simulation. This is because, although radiation transport
plays an important role in the later stages of the inertial connement fusion proces, its
eects are not as pronounced in the earlier phases. For this reason, computational ef-
ciency was prioritized over strict physical acuracy. Tabulated equation-of-state data
of both DT and CH were generated from MPQEOS code. The implicit heat transport
module with BiCGSTAB solver described in Section 2.1.2 is used.

4. Conclusions
In this paper, a SPH-based RHD code SPRAY is presented. It is a particle-based,
mesh-fre, Lagrangian code intended to simulate long pulse high-intensity laser-plasma
interaction in HEDP regime. It utilizes GPU for its masively paralel aproach, and
its SPH foundation gives it an edge on traditionaly chalenging isues such as tracking
uid surfaces and simulating complex deformations, which usualy necesitated heav-
ily time-consuming numerical techniques. An algorithm suitable for GPU paraleliza-
tion aceleration is implemented in the nearest neighbor particle search (NPS) routine
for optimal performance. The SPH formulations are tailored toward simulating laser-
target interaction, thus yielding acurate and reliable results. A novel particle-based
laser ray-tracing scheme is also developed with integration with the SPH foundation in

The versatility and reliability of the code is veried with a series of benchmarks.
First, the validity of the hydrodynamics calculation as wel as the ability to capture and
resolve shock waves is conrmed with the Sod shock tube benchmark as the simulation
results are in god agrement with the analytical solution. Second, the radiation trans-
port routine and the coupling of laser energy to the plasma are validated by comparing
the simulation results with a wel-established code MULTI-IFE[1]. The density, ve-
locity, ion/electron temperature prole evolution calculated by SPRAY closely matched
that of the reference code. Third, the code’s ability to model multidimensional insta-
bilities was examined with the clasical Rayleigh-Taylor instability benchmark. The
growth rate of the spike and the buble was compared with that of a reference code
ATHENA[82], along with the linear theory predictions. The results from SPRAY are
shown to exhibit the initial linear phase growth, and are sucesful in reproducing the
reference code’s results at various resolutions. Fourth, simulation of implosion of an
ICF target is caried out to ilustrate a potential aplication of SPRAY code. The ex-
pected growth of the instabilities as wel as turbulent mixing phenomena are clearly
observed, thus demonstrating the robustnes of the code. Fifth, a laser-driven implo-
sion simulation results are shown, which exhibiting the capability of ful multidimen-
sional laser ray-tracing routine coupled with the code. Only two-dimensional results
are included in this study, as the extension to thre dimensions is left as a future work.
There are several clear limitations of the SPRAY code. First, there are inherent
restrictions steming from using SPH methods in the context of high energy density
physics. Drastic changes in the state of mater, i.e. phase change from solids to plasmas
via laser ablation, are notoriously chalenging to model. Thanks to years of eort and
research, Eulerian aproaches have more or les matured in terms of modeling such
phase changes, but it remains one of the grand chalenges of SPH.
Second, there is rom for improvement of the implementation of radiation transport
solver. As stated in this paper, SPRAY code solves the radiation transport equations
derived with the gray aproximation. The physical acuracy of the model would cer-
tainly improve if the code were to be extended to suport multigroup aproximation,
especialy when modeling indirectly driven inertial connement fusion where strong
X-rays act as the driver. Moreover, although the ux-limited diusion aproach yields
reasonable results in both the opticaly thick and thin limits, it breaks down in the inter-
mediate regime. A more realistic modeling could be achieved with improved methods
such as the variable Edington method[35]. Furthermore, a more modern numerical
solver could increase both the performance and scalability of the Jacobi-based implicit
solver implemented in the code. It is expected that a more computationaly ecient
scheme could dramaticaly reduce the number of iterations required for convergence
by orders of magnitude.
To the authors’ knowledge, this is the rst atempt to aply SPH techniques to
HEDP research involving laser-target interactions. Therefore, the signicance of this
research lies in the fact that it opens posibility of tackling chalenging isues in the
HEDP eld with the rapidly advancing numerical analysis capabilities and techniques
of SPH. Works in progres that would be implemented in future releases include laser
beam-beam interaction modeling, as wel as high-performance and highly optimized

implemented properly, would enable SPRAY to adres its curent limitations and be
aplicable to even broader range of HEDP numerical studies.

Abstract: Here we report the development of SPRAY, a masively paralel GPU acelerated, smothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH)-based, radiation hydrodynamics (RHD) code designed specicaly for simulating high intensity laser-plasma interactions. When a target is iradiated by an intense laser, highly complex uid deformation ocurs due to instabilities, which is chalenging to study numericaly. SPRAY is particle-based, mesh-fre, and Lagrangian, which adreses numerical isues that posed diculties to existing methods. Its SPH formulations for RHD governing equations are tailored toward acurate and reliable simulations of laser-target iradiation phenomena, and are solved via a time-dependent, ux-limited di usion method. A new laser energy coupling module, which is based on the Wentzel-Kramers-Brilouin (WKB) aproxi- mation, is implemented with a totaly mesh-fre ray-tracing scheme that is aplicable for arbitrary geometry and dimensions. The acuracy and reliability of the code are demonstrated with a series of benchmark problems. To the authors’ knowledge, this is the rst atempt to employ SPH method for simulations of laser-plasma interactions in high energy density physics research. Posible expansions to the code, such as laser beam-beam interaction modeling and more sophisticated multi-group radiation trans- port are left for future development.
